A. Metaphysis and growth plate
B. Epiphysis only
C. Diaphysis and physis
D. Physis and epiphysis
E. Entire physis
Answer: A. Salter–Harris II involves the growth plate and metaphysis, with a triangular metaphyseal fragment being characteristic.
6. A 40-year-old man in an RTC presents hypotensive with pelvic instability and pelvic pain. Initial FAST shows free fluid in the pelvis. What is the most appropriate next step?
A. Apply pelvic binder immediately
B. CT abdomen without binder
C. Straight to interventional radiology
D. Immediate laparotomy
E. Conservative observation
Answer: A. In unstable pelvic fractures, applying a pelvic binder promptly can temporarily reduce pelvic volume and control bleeding, aligning with ATLS and NICE trauma guidelines.
7. A 25-year-old man after blunt abdominal trauma has a tender abdomen, positive FAST, and a stable BP. What’s the best next step?
A. Immediate laparotomy
B. Urgent CT abdomen
C. Diagnostic peritoneal lavage (DPL)
D. Serial abdominal exams
E. Start NSAIDs and observe
Answer: B. In a stable trauma patient with a positive FAST, CT abdomen is the recommended next step to identify visceral injuries as per NICE/ATLS protocols.
8. A 30-year-old has a tibial shaft fracture with escalating pain out of proportion to exam, pain with passive stretch, and tense calf. What is the next best step?
A. Start NSAIDs
B. Elevate limb and observe
C. Measure compartment pressures
D. Provide analgesia only
E. Perform fasciotomy
Answer: C. When clinical suspicion is high, measuring intracompartmental pressure is essential to confirm compartment syndrome before proceeding to fasciotomy.
9. A 25-year-old with a Gustilo–Anderson grade II open tibial fracture occurs after a farm accident. What initial management is appropriate within the first hour?
A. Cast immobilisation only
B. IV antibiotics (cefuroxime + gentamicin) and tetanus prophylaxis and urgent debridement
C. Oral antibiotics
D. Urgent external fixation
E. Delayed surgical review
Answer: B. For grade II open fractures, immediate IV antibiotics and tetanus cover, with surgical debridement within 6 hours, is recommended by NICE.
10. A 22-year-old rugby player falls onto an outstretched arm, with the shoulder held in abduction and external rotation. Radiographs show an anterior glenohumeral dislocation. What does ATLS recommend as the next step?
A. Immediate closed reduction under sedation
B. Delay reduction until CT obtained
C. Begin physiotherapy
D. Sling only
E. Open reduction under GA
Answer: A. Anterior shoulder dislocations should be promptly reduced under analgesia/sedation to alleviate pain and restore anatomy per ATLS principles.
11. A 30-year‑old pedestrian was brought in after being struck by a car. He presents with a flexed, adducted, and internally rotated hip. He is hemodynamically stable. Radiographs confirm a posterior hip dislocation.
A. CT scan before reduction
B. Immediate closed reduction under anaesthesia
C. Prolonged traction
D. Total hip replacement
E. Conservative management
Answer: B. NICE and ATLS guidelines advise prompt closed reduction under sedation/anaesthesia for posterior hip dislocations to minimise the risk of avascular necrosis.
12. A 22-year‑old rugby player fell onto his shoulder in a match and holds his arm slightly abducted and externally rotated. Radiograph confirms an anterior glenohumeral dislocation.
A. Immediate closed reduction under sedation
B. Immobilise for 4 weeks without reduction
C. CT scan before reduction
D. Physiotherapy only
E. Emergency arthroscopy
Answer: A. Prompt reduction under pain relief/sedation is recommended in acute anterior shoulder dislocations per NICE and ATLS guidelines.
13. A 45-year‑old patient’s knee dislocation was reduced, but distal pulses remain diminished.
A. CT angiogram
B. Physiotherapy back to baseline
C. No further imaging
D. Chiropractic adjustment
E. Ranger brace therapy 
Answer: A. Persistent pulse deficit demands immediate CT angiography to assess for vascular injury and guide treatment.
14. A middle-aged office worker falls onto an outstretched hand and presents with a visibly shortened, dorsally angulated wrist after radiographs confirm a distal radius fracture. The fracture is displaced by more than 10° of dorsal tilt and >2 mm radial shortening. What is the most appropriate next step?
A. Immobilise in a removable splint and outpatient follow-up
B. Immediate closed reduction and below-elbow cast under analgesia
C. Internal fixation with plate under GA
D. Accept deformity and manage conservatively
E. External fixation only 
Answer: B. Guidelines recommend closed reduction under appropriate analgesia or sedation for displaced distal radius fractures, followed by immobilisation in a below-elbow cast pending follow-up imaging.

15. A 70-year-old patient on warfarin falls and sustains a minimally displaced distal radius fracture, with AP and lateral X-rays showing less than 10° dorsal tilt. Which management aligns with current guidance?
A. Immediate reduction in A&E
B. Conservative management in wrist splint and arrange imaging follow-up
C. Immediate surgical fixation
D. External fixation due to warfarin
E. Manipulation under anaesthesia
Answer: B. Minimally displaced distal radius fractures in low-risk patients can be managed conservatively with a splint and arranged review, consistent with fracture management recommendations.

16. A teenager presents after a fall onto an outstretched hand with tenderness over the scaphoid but a normal initial X-ray. What is the appropriate management?
A. Discharge home with advice
B. Splint in a navicular cast and repeat imaging in 10–14 days
C. Immediate MRI
D. Open surgical fixation
E. Ignore as X-ray is normal
Answer: B. Suspicious scaphoid injury with normal initial X-ray requires immobilisation in a scaphoid cast and repeat imaging or MRI within 10–14 days as per guidelines

17. A 34-year-old athlete presents after an acute patellar dislocation. Which imaging assessment is recommended to evaluate bony anatomy prior to physiotherapy?
MRI or CT
X-ray only
C. Bone scan
D. Ultrasound
E. No imaging
Answer: A. MRI or CT is advised to assess bony alignment (i.e., tibial-tubercle–trochlear groove distance, trochlear morphology) before definitive therapy.

18. A 30-year-old patient has a seizure. After the seizure terminates, they present with shoulder pain and his arm held in internal rotation after a convulsion. Movement is extremely limited. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A. Anterior shoulder dislocation
B. Posterior shoulder dislocation
C. Clavicle fracture
D. Rotator cuff tear
E. AC joint sprain
Answer: B. The presentation—arm internally rotated and limited external rotation—strongly suggests posterior shoulder dislocation, a frequently missed diagnosis requiring prompt recognition and reduction.

19. A 24-year-old motorcyclist comes in post high-speed crash complaining of severe neck pain. Imaging shows dislocation of one facet joint on lateral C-spine film. What is the classification and next step?
A. Unifacet C-spine dislocation; immobilise and urgent CT + MRI
B. Bilateral facet; conservative management
C. Compression fracture only; physiotherapy
D. C1 burst; traction
E. No significant injury; discharge
Answer: A. Unifacet cervical dislocation is unstable and mandates immobilisation plus urgent CT/MRI, as per NICE trauma guidelines.

20. An 8-year-old falls onto an outstretched arm and presents with lateral elbow tenderness and limited range of motion; X-ray shows a fracture through the lateral epicondyle apophysis. What is the correct treatment approach?
A. Non-operative with long-arm cast
B. Immediate ORIF
C. Humeral plating
D. Sling only
E. Elbow arthroscopy
Answer: A. Lateral epicondyle fractures in children are typically treated non-operatively with immobilisation unless displaced >2 mm or causing instability.
21. An 84-year-old woman is brought to A&E after falling at home. She is unable to weight-bear, and her left leg is shortened and externally rotated. Pelvic X-rays show a displaced intracapsular fracture of the left femoral neck. She has mild dementia and limited mobility. What is the most appropriate management?
A. Cannulated screw fixation
B. Total hip replacement
C. Dynamic hip screw
D. Hemiarthroplasty
E. Non-operative management
Answer: D. In elderly patients with cognitive impairment and reduced function, guidelines recommend hemiarthroplasty for displaced intracapsular hip fractures.

22. A 72-year-old man with good mobility and no cognitive impairment presents with a displaced intracapsular hip fracture after a fall. What surgical treatment is most appropriate?
A. Cannulated screw fixation
B. Hemiarthroplasty
C. Total hip replacement
D. External fixation
E. Intramedullary nail
Answer: C. Patients who are functionally independent and cognitively intact are suitable for total hip replacement

23. A 25-year-old man presents after a fall from height with groin pain and inability to walk. Imaging reveals an undisplaced intracapsular femoral neck fracture. What is the preferred management approach?
A. Dynamic hip screw
B. Total hip replacement
C. Hemiarthroplasty
D. Cannulated screw fixation
E. Conservative treatment
Answer: D. Young patients with undisplaced intracapsular fractures are managed with cannulated screws to preserve the femoral head.

24. A 79-year-old woman with a history of hypertension falls on stairs and sustains an intertrochanteric femur fracture. She is fully independent. What surgical approach is most appropriate?
A. Cannulated screw fixation
B. Dynamic hip screw
C. Total hip replacement
D. External fixation
E. Hemiarthroplasty
Answer: B. Stable intertrochanteric fractures are treated with dynamic hip screws, providing stability and promoting healing.

25. A 30-year-old male is evaluated for an intracapsular femoral neck fracture. Why is surgical fixation preferred over arthroplasty in this case?
A. Cost-effectiveness
B. Cosmetic outcome
C. Reduced risk of avascular necrosis
D. Preservation of native femoral head
E. Lower pain scores
Answer: D. Preservation of the femoral head is critical in younger patients to maintain long-term joint function.
26. A 62-year-old woman falls on her outstretched hand. X-ray shows an extra-articular distal radius fracture with 5° dorsal angulation and no shortening. What is the most appropriate management?
A. Below-elbow cast and outpatient follow-up
B. Immediate volar plate fixation
C. K-wire fixation
D. External fixation
E. Surgery in two weeks
Answer: A. This minimally displaced, extra-articular fracture can be managed non-operatively with a cast

27. A 28-year-old man with a high-energy fall has an intra-articular distal radius fracture with >2 mm articular stepoff. Which management is indicated?
A. Removable splint
B. Closed reduction only
C. Surgical fixation with volar plate
D. Immobilisation for six weeks
E. K-wire and cast
Answer: C. Intra-articular fractures with stepoff require anatomical reduction and fixation, usually with a volar plate, to restore joint congruity.
28. A 14-year-old boy sustains a minimally displaced distal radius fracture with 10° volar angulation. Radiographs show growth plate is intact. How should this be managed?
A. Volar plating
B. K-wire fixation
C. Cast in flexion
D. Non-operative management
E. Immediate physiotherapy
Answer: D. Minimally displaced paediatric fractures can be treated conservatively with casting.
29. A 67-year-old woman has a dorsally angulated distal radius fracture of 15°, extra-articular. After reduction, alignment improves to <5° dorsally. What treatment should follow?
A. Volar plating
B. K-wires
C. Cast immobilisation
D. Ankle plate
E. External fixation
Answer: C. Acceptable alignment after closed reduction allows for cast immobilisation without surgical intervention.
30. A 72-year-old with osteoporosis presents with an unstable, comminuted distal radius fracture, with dorsal angulation >20°. What is the most appropriate operative method?
A. Cast only
B. K-wire fixation
C. Volar locked plating
D. External fixator
E. Conservative management
Answer: C. Unstable, comminuted fractures benefit from volar plate fixation to maintain alignment and allow early mobilisation.
31. A 22-year-old male sustains a tibial shaft fracture in a motorbike crash. Eight hours later he complains of worsening calf pain, worse on passive stretch, and his toes feel tight. What is the immediate next step?
A. Start NSAIDs and observe
B. Remove cast or dressing and measure compartment pressure
C. Elevate limb and recheck tomorrow
D. Prescribe physiotherapy
E. Apply a tighter compression bandage
Answer: B. In suspected compartment syndrome, promptly remove external compression and measure compartment pressures to confirm diagnosis before fasciotomy.

32. A 45-year-old construction worker develops intense leg pain out of proportion after tibial fracture treatment; pressure monitoring shows delta pressure (diastolic – compartment) of 25 mmHg. What is your next step in management?
A. NSAIDs and elevation
B. Immediate fasciotomy
C. Cast adjustment
D. Oral analgesia
E. Physiotherapy
Answer: B. A delta pressure ≤30 mmHg confirms compartment syndrome—urgent fasciotomy is essential to prevent tissue necrosis.
33. A 25-year-old farmer presents with a Grade I open tibial shaft fracture following machinery injury. Immediate management?
A. Oral antibiotics and splint
B. IV antibiotics (cefuroxime), tetanus, splint, debridement within 6 h
C. Cast with outpatient follow-up
D. IV analgesia only
E. No IV fluids
Answer: B. All open fractures require IV antibiotics, tetanus prophylaxis, immobilisation, and timely debridement as per NICE.
34. A 40-year-old with a Grade IIIa open femur fracture has moderate soft tissue loss and bone contamination. What is key management?
A. Delay debridement
B. Early debridement, IV antibiotics, and definitive fixation
C. Cast only
D. Oral antibiotics only
E. Physiotherapy alone
Answer: B. Grade IIIa injuries need emergent debridement, broad-spectrum antibiotics (± gentamicin), and early surgical fixation.
35. A 30-year-old motorcyclist presents after a road accident with a mid-shaft humeral fracture. He reports wrist drop and inability to extend the wrist and fingers. Which nerve is most likely injured?
A. Axillary
B. Radial
C. Ulnar
D. Median
E. Sciatic
Answer: B. Wrist drop and inability to extend the wrist/fingers point to radial nerve palsy, commonly injured in mid-shaft humeral fractures.
36. A 45-year-old construction worker falls from scaffolding and lands on his shoulder. He has absent sensation over the lateral shoulder and cannot abduct beyond 15°. Which nerve is affected?
A. Ulnar
B. Radial
C. Sciatic
D. Axillary
E. Peroneal
Answer: D. Loss of shoulder abduction (deltoid) and lateral shoulder sensation indicates axillary nerve injury after shoulder trauma.

37. A 40-year-old office manager falls onto an outstretched hand, injuring his wrist. He reports numbness in the radial half of the palm and thumb opposition weakness. Which nerve is most likely compromised?
A. Ulnar
B. Median
C. Radial
D. Axillary
E. Femoral
Answer: B. Median nerve injury presents with sensory loss in the palmar thumb area and thenar weakness.
38. A 35-year-old football player falls onto his knee during a match and develops foot drop with reduced dorsiflexion and eversion. Which nerve is most likely injured?
A. Femoral
B. Tibial
C. Sciatic
D. Common peroneal
E. Median
Answer: D. Foot drop with dorsiflexion and eversion weakness indicates common peroneal nerve injury at the fibular head.
39. A 34-year-old motorcyclist involved in high-speed collision arrives complaining of neck pain and reduced movement. Neurological exam is normal. What is the most appropriate initial action?
A. Remove helmet and encourage movement
B. Apply cervical collar and spinal board before imaging
C. Immediately order MRI
D. Allow normal posture
E. Provide analgesia only
Answer: B. Immediate immobilisation with a cervical collar and spinal board is essential to prevent further injury until imaging is performed.

40. A 55-year-old pedestrian struck by a car presents with torticollis and neck stiffness. Lateral C-spine X-ray shows anterior subluxation of C5 on C6 with widening of the spinous processes. What injury pattern is this?
A. Unilateral facet dislocation
B. Bilateral facet dislocation
C. Compression fracture
D. Odontoid fracture
E. Atlantoaxial rotatory subluxation
Answer: B. Anterior displacement with spinous widening indicates bilateral facet dislocation, a highly unstable injury.

41. A 28-year-old rock climber falls 3 meters. CT scan shows fracture through the transverse foramen of C6 without displacement. What is the correct classification?
A. Odontoid fracture
B. Lateral mass fracture
C. Jefferson fracture
D. Unstable hangman’s fracture
E. Transverse process fracture
Answer: E. Fracture of the transverse process/foramen is typically considered a stable injury, often with vertebral artery risk.

42. A 19-year-old rugby player lands on his head during a scrum. He is alert but reports neck pain. What is the next step in radiographic assessment?
A. Only lateral X-ray
B. AP, lateral, odontoid and CT if any abnormal
C. MRI only
D. Cervical ultrasound
E. No imaging needed
Answer: B. Initial imaging should include the “neck collar” views (AP, lateral, odontoid) and CT for suspected injury to aid diagnosis.

43. A 47-year-old has C-spine immobilised with a hard collar only, after a high-speed collision. MRI later shows interspinous ligament rupture but no fracture. What immobilisation strategy is indicated?
A. Collar removed
B. Continue collar
C. Rigid halo orthosis
D. Bed rest only
E. Cervical traction
Answer: C. Ligamentous injury without fracture needs rigid immobilisation, such as a halo vest, for effective stabilisation.

44. A 7-year-old boy falls onto his outstretched hand and sustains a greenstick fracture of the distal radius. What anatomical difference explains this injury pattern?
A. Children have thicker periosteum allowing bending fractures
B. Adults have more elastic bones
C. Children lack periosteum
D. Adults have more vascular bones
E. Children have brittle bones
Answer: A. Thicker periosteum in children allows bending injuries like greenstick fractures that rarely occur in adults.
45. An 11-year-old girl with a fall has a buckle (torus) fracture of the tibia. Which property explains its formation?
A. Bones are softer and more pliable
B. Bones are brittle
C. Lack of periosteum
D. Bones are rigid
E. High bone density
Answer: A. Paediatric bones are more flexible, leading to buckle fractures under compressive forces.
46. A 12-year-old boy presents after twisting his ankle; X-ray shows a fracture that crosses the physis without metaphyseal or epiphyseal involvement. What Salter–Harris type is this?
A. Type I
B. Type II
C. Type III
D. Type IV
E. Type V
Answer: A. Type I injuries traverse the growth plate only, true to the Salter-Harris classification.
47. A 14-year-old girl has a distal femur fracture extending through metaphysis and physis but sparing the epiphysis. What type is it?
A. Type I
B. Type II
C. Type III
D. Type IV
E. Type V
Answer: B. Type II fractures involve the metaphysis and physis, sparing the epiphysis.
48. A 13-year-old boy fractures the distal tibial physis and epiphysis through the joint surface. What Salter–Harris type describes this?
A. Type III
B. Type I
C. Type II
D. Type IV
E. Type V
Answer: A. Type III injuries traverse the physis and enter the epiphysis, affecting the joint surface.
49. A 46-year-old has a distal radius fracture treated with K-wires. What is the primary advantage of K-wire fixation?
A. Provides load-bearing support
B. Minimally invasive, temporary stabilisation
C. Permanent fracture fixation
D. Replaces wrist joint
E. Allows immediate weight-bearing
Answer: B. K-wires offer minimally invasive fixation, ideal for less complex distal radius fractures.
 
50. A patient with a distal radius fracture has a volar plate implanted. What is the main benefit of plate fixation over K-wires?
A. Avoids hospitalisation
B. Rigid fixation, earlier motion
C. Less invasive than K-wires
D. Cheaper
E. No need for physiotherapy
Answer: B. Volar plates provide stable fixation, facilitating early rehabilitation and better alignment.

Answer: B. In a stable trauma patient with a positive FAST, CT abdomen is the recommended next step to identify visceral injuries as per NICE/ATLS protocols.
A 30-year-old has a tibial shaft fracture with escalating pain out of proportion to exam, pain with passive stretch, and tense calf. What is the next best step?
A. Start NSAIDs
B. Elevate limb and observe
C. Measure compartment pressures
D. Provide analgesia only
E. Perform fasciotomy
Answer: C. When clinical suspicion is high, measuring intracompartmental pressure is essential to confirm compartment syndrome before proceeding to fasciotomy.
A 25-year-old with a Gustilo–Anderson grade II open tibial fracture occurs after a farm accident. What initial management is appropriate within the first hour?
A. Cast immobilisation only
B. IV antibiotics (cefuroxime + gentamicin) and tetanus prophylaxis and urgent debridement
C. Oral antibiotics
D. Urgent external fixation
E. Delayed surgical review
Answer: B. For grade II open fractures, immediate IV antibiotics and tetanus cover, with surgical debridement within 6 hours, is recommended by NICE.
A 22-year-old rugby player falls onto an outstretched arm, with the shoulder held in abduction and external rotation. Radiographs show an anterior glenohumeral dislocation. What does ATLS recommend as the next step?
A. Immediate closed reduction under sedation
B. Delay reduction until CT obtained
C. Begin physiotherapy
D. Sling only
E. Open reduction under GA
Answer: A. Anterior shoulder dislocations should be promptly reduced under analgesia/sedation to alleviate pain and restore anatomy per ATLS principles.
A 30-year‑old pedestrian was brought in after being struck by a car. He presents with a flexed, adducted, and internally rotated hip. He is hemodynamically stable. Radiographs confirm a posterior hip dislocation.
A. CT scan before reduction
B. Immediate closed reduction under anaesthesia
C. Prolonged traction
D. Total hip replacement
E. Conservative management
Answer: B. NICE and ATLS guidelines advise prompt closed reduction under sedation/anaesthesia for posterior hip dislocations to minimise the risk of avascular necrosis.
A 22-year‑old rugby player fell onto his shoulder in a match and holds his arm slightly abducted and externally rotated. Radiograph confirms an anterior glenohumeral dislocation.
A. Immediate closed reduction under sedation
B. Immobilise for 4 weeks without reduction
C. CT scan before reduction
D. Physiotherapy only
E. Emergency arthroscopy
Answer: A. Prompt reduction under pain relief/sedation is recommended in acute anterior shoulder dislocations per NICE and ATLS guidelines.
A 45-year‑old patient’s knee dislocation was reduced, but distal pulses remain diminished.
A. CT angiogram
B. Physiotherapy back to baseline
C. No further imaging
D. Chiropractic adjustment
E. Ranger brace therapy 
Answer: A. Persistent pulse deficit demands immediate CT angiography to assess for vascular injury and guide treatment.
A middle-aged office worker falls onto an outstretched hand and presents with a visibly shortened, dorsally angulated wrist after radiographs confirm a distal radius fracture. The fracture is displaced by more than 10° of dorsal tilt and >2 mm radial shortening. What is the most appropriate next step?
A. Immobilise in a removable splint and outpatient follow-up
B. Immediate closed reduction and below-elbow cast under analgesia
C. Internal fixation with plate under GA
D. Accept deformity and manage conservatively
E. External fixation only 
Answer: B. Guidelines recommend closed reduction under appropriate analgesia or sedation for displaced distal radius fractures, followed by immobilisation in a below-elbow cast pending follow-up imaging.

A 70-year-old patient on warfarin falls and sustains a minimally displaced distal radius fracture, with AP and lateral X-rays showing less than 10° dorsal tilt. Which management aligns with current guidance?
A. Immediate reduction in A&E
B. Conservative management in wrist splint and arrange imaging follow-up
C. Immediate surgical fixation
D. External fixation due to warfarin
E. Manipulation under anaesthesia
Answer: B. Minimally displaced distal radius fractures in low-risk patients can be managed conservatively with a splint and arranged review, consistent with fracture management recommendations.

A teenager presents after a fall onto an outstretched hand with tenderness over the scaphoid but a normal initial X-ray. What is the appropriate management?
A. Discharge home with advice
B. Splint in a navicular cast and repeat imaging in 10–14 days
C. Immediate MRI
D. Open surgical fixation
E. Ignore as X-ray is normal
Answer: B. Suspicious scaphoid injury with normal initial X-ray requires immobilisation in a scaphoid cast and repeat imaging or MRI within 10–14 days as per guidelines

A 34-year-old athlete presents after an acute patellar dislocation. Which imaging assessment is recommended to evaluate bony anatomy prior to physiotherapy?
MRI or CT
X-ray only
C. Bone scan
D. Ultrasound
E. No imaging
Answer: A. MRI or CT is advised to assess bony alignment (i.e., tibial-tubercle–trochlear groove distance, trochlear morphology) before definitive therapy.

A 30-year-old patient has a seizure. After the seizure terminates, they present with shoulder pain and his arm held in internal rotation after a convulsion. Movement is extremely limited. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A. Anterior shoulder dislocation
B. Posterior shoulder dislocation
C. Clavicle fracture
D. Rotator cuff tear
E. AC joint sprain
Answer: B. The presentation—arm internally rotated and limited external rotation—strongly suggests posterior shoulder dislocation, a frequently missed diagnosis requiring prompt recognition and reduction.

A 24-year-old motorcyclist comes in post high-speed crash complaining of severe neck pain. Imaging shows dislocation of one facet joint on lateral C-spine film. What is the classification and next step?
A. Unifacet C-spine dislocation; immobilise and urgent CT + MRI
B. Bilateral facet; conservative management
C. Compression fracture only; physiotherapy
D. C1 burst; traction
E. No significant injury; discharge
Answer: A. Unifacet cervical dislocation is unstable and mandates immobilisation plus urgent CT/MRI, as per NICE trauma guidelines.

An 8-year-old falls onto an outstretched arm and presents with lateral elbow tenderness and limited range of motion; X-ray shows a fracture through the lateral epicondyle apophysis. What is the correct treatment approach?
A. Non-operative with long-arm cast
B. Immediate ORIF
C. Humeral plating
D. Sling only
E. Elbow arthroscopy
Answer: A. Lateral epicondyle fractures in children are typically treated non-operatively with immobilisation unless displaced >2 mm or causing instability.
An 84-year-old woman is brought to A&E after falling at home. She is unable to weight-bear, and her left leg is shortened and externally rotated. Pelvic X-rays show a displaced intracapsular fracture of the left femoral neck. She has mild dementia and limited mobility. What is the most appropriate management?
A. Cannulated screw fixation
B. Total hip replacement
C. Dynamic hip screw
D. Hemiarthroplasty
E. Non-operative management
Answer: D.
In elderly patients with cognitive impairment and reduced function, guidelines recommend hemiarthroplasty for displaced intracapsular hip fractures.

A 72-year-old man with good mobility and no cognitive impairment presents with a displaced intracapsular hip fracture after a fall. What surgical treatment is most appropriate?
A. Cannulated screw fixation
B. Hemiarthroplasty
C. Total hip replacement
D. External fixation
E. Intramedullary nail
Answer: C.
Patients who are functionally independent and cognitively intact are suitable for total hip replacement

A 25-year-old man presents after a fall from height with groin pain and inability to walk. Imaging reveals an undisplaced intracapsular femoral neck fracture. What is the preferred management approach?
A. Dynamic hip screw
B. Total hip replacement
C. Hemiarthroplasty
D. Cannulated screw fixation
E. Conservative treatment
Answer: D.
Young patients with undisplaced intracapsular fractures are managed with cannulated screws to preserve the femoral head.

A 79-year-old woman with a history of hypertension falls on stairs and sustains an intertrochanteric femur fracture. She is fully independent. What surgical approach is most appropriate?
A. Cannulated screw fixation
B. Dynamic hip screw
C. Total hip replacement
D. External fixation
E. Hemiarthroplasty
Answer: B.
Stable intertrochanteric fractures are treated with dynamic hip screws, providing stability and promoting healing.

A 30-year-old male is evaluated for an intracapsular femoral neck fracture. Why is surgical fixation preferred over arthroplasty in this case?
A. Cost-effectiveness
B. Cosmetic outcome
C. Reduced risk of avascular necrosis
D. Preservation of native femoral head
E. Lower pain scores
Answer: D.
Preservation of the femoral head is critical in younger patients to maintain long-term joint function.
A 62-year-old woman falls on her outstretched hand. X-ray shows an extra-articular distal radius fracture with 5° dorsal angulation and no shortening. What is the most appropriate management?
A. Below-elbow cast and outpatient follow-up
B. Immediate volar plate fixation
C. K-wire fixation
D. External fixation
E. Surgery in two weeks
Answer: A. This minimally displaced, extra-articular fracture can be managed non-operatively with a cast

A 28-year-old man with a high-energy fall has an intra-articular distal radius fracture with >2 mm articular stepoff. Which management is indicated?
A. Removable splint
B. Closed reduction only
C. Surgical fixation with volar plate
D. Immobilisation for six weeks
E. K-wire and cast
Answer: C. Intra-articular fractures with stepoff require anatomical reduction and fixation, usually with a volar plate, to restore joint congruity.
A 14-year-old boy sustains a minimally displaced distal radius fracture with 10° volar angulation. Radiographs show growth plate is intact. How should this be managed?
A. Volar plating
B. K-wire fixation
C. Cast in flexion
D. Non-operative management
E. Immediate physiotherapy
Answer: D. Minimally displaced paediatric fractures can be treated conservatively with casting.
A 67-year-old woman has a dorsally angulated distal radius fracture of 15°, extra-articular. After reduction, alignment improves to <5° dorsally. What treatment should follow?
A. Volar plating
B. K-wires
C. Cast immobilisation
D. Ankle plate
E. External fixation
Answer: C. Acceptable alignment after closed reduction allows for cast immobilisation without surgical intervention.
A 72-year-old with osteoporosis presents with an unstable, comminuted distal radius fracture, with dorsal angulation >20°. What is the most appropriate operative method?
A. Cast only
B. K-wire fixation
C. Volar locked plating
D. External fixator
E. Conservative management
Answer: C. Unstable, comminuted fractures benefit from volar plate fixation to maintain alignment and allow early mobilisation.
A 22-year-old male sustains a tibial shaft fracture in a motorbike crash. Eight hours later he complains of worsening calf pain, worse on passive stretch, and his toes feel tight. What is the immediate next step?
A. Start NSAIDs and observe
B. Remove cast or dressing and measure compartment pressure
C. Elevate limb and recheck tomorrow
D. Prescribe physiotherapy
E. Apply a tighter compression bandage
Answer: B. In suspected compartment syndrome, promptly remove external compression and measure compartment pressures to confirm diagnosis before fasciotomy.

A 45-year-old construction worker develops intense leg pain out of proportion after tibial fracture treatment; pressure monitoring shows delta pressure (diastolic – compartment) of 25 mmHg. What is your next step in management?
A. NSAIDs and elevation
B. Immediate fasciotomy
C. Cast adjustment
D. Oral analgesia
E. Physiotherapy
Answer: B. A delta pressure ≤30 mmHg confirms compartment syndrome—urgent fasciotomy is essential to prevent tissue necrosis.
A 25-year-old farmer presents with a Grade I open tibial shaft fracture following machinery injury. Immediate management?
A. Oral antibiotics and splint
B. IV antibiotics (cefuroxime), tetanus, splint, debridement within 6 h
C. Cast with outpatient follow-up
D. IV analgesia only
E. No IV fluids
Answer: B. All open fractures require IV antibiotics, tetanus prophylaxis, immobilisation, and timely debridement as per NICE.
A 40-year-old with a Grade IIIa open femur fracture has moderate soft tissue loss and bone contamination. What is key management?
A. Delay debridement
B. Early debridement, IV antibiotics, and definitive fixation
C. Cast only
D. Oral antibiotics only
E. Physiotherapy alone
Answer: B. Grade IIIa injuries need emergent debridement, broad-spectrum antibiotics (± gentamicin), and early surgical fixation.
A 30-year-old motorcyclist presents after a road accident with a mid-shaft humeral fracture. He reports wrist drop and inability to extend the wrist and fingers. Which nerve is most likely injured?
A. Axillary
B. Radial
C. Ulnar
D. Median
E. Sciatic
Answer: B.
Wrist drop and inability to extend the wrist/fingers point to radial nerve palsy, commonly injured in mid-shaft humeral fractures.
A 45-year-old construction worker falls from scaffolding and lands on his shoulder. He has absent sensation over the lateral shoulder and cannot abduct beyond 15°. Which nerve is affected?
A. Ulnar
B. Radial
C. Sciatic
D. Axillary
E. Peroneal
Answer: D.
Loss of shoulder abduction (deltoid) and lateral shoulder sensation indicates axillary nerve injury after shoulder trauma.

A 40-year-old office manager falls onto an outstretched hand, injuring his wrist. He reports numbness in the radial half of the palm and thumb opposition weakness. Which nerve is most likely compromised?
A. Ulnar
B. Median
C. Radial
D. Axillary
E. Femoral
Answer: B.
Median nerve injury presents with sensory loss in the palmar thumb area and thenar weakness.
A 35-year-old football player falls onto his knee during a match and develops foot drop with reduced dorsiflexion and eversion. Which nerve is most likely injured?
A. Femoral
B. Tibial
C. Sciatic
D. Common peroneal
E. Median
Answer: D.
Foot drop with dorsiflexion and eversion weakness indicates common peroneal nerve injury at the fibular head.
A 34-year-old motorcyclist involved in high-speed collision arrives complaining of neck pain and reduced movement. Neurological exam is normal. What is the most appropriate initial action?
A. Remove helmet and encourage movement
B. Apply cervical collar and spinal board before imaging
C. Immediately order MRI
D. Allow normal posture
E. Provide analgesia only
Answer: B.
Immediate immobilisation with a cervical collar and spinal board is essential to prevent further injury until imaging is performed.

A 55-year-old pedestrian struck by a car presents with torticollis and neck stiffness. Lateral C-spine X-ray shows anterior subluxation of C5 on C6 with widening of the spinous processes. What injury pattern is this?
A. Unilateral facet dislocation
B. Bilateral facet dislocation
C. Compression fracture
D. Odontoid fracture
E. Atlantoaxial rotatory subluxation
Answer: B.
Anterior displacement with spinous widening indicates bilateral facet dislocation, a highly unstable injury.

A 28-year-old rock climber falls 3 meters. CT scan shows fracture through the transverse foramen of C6 without displacement. What is the correct classification?
A. Odontoid fracture
B. Lateral mass fracture
C. Jefferson fracture
D. Unstable hangman’s fracture
E. Transverse process fracture
Answer: E.
Fracture of the transverse process/foramen is typically considered a stable injury, often with vertebral artery risk.

A 19-year-old rugby player lands on his head during a scrum. He is alert but reports neck pain. What is the next step in radiographic assessment?
A. Only lateral X-ray
B. AP, lateral, odontoid and CT if any abnormal
C. MRI only
D. Cervical ultrasound
E. No imaging needed
Answer: B.
Initial imaging should include the “neck collar” views (AP, lateral, odontoid) and CT for suspected injury to aid diagnosis.

A 47-year-old has C-spine immobilised with a hard collar only, after a high-speed collision. MRI later shows interspinous ligament rupture but no fracture. What immobilisation strategy is indicated?
A. Collar removed
B. Continue collar
C. Rigid halo orthosis
D. Bed rest only
E. Cervical traction
Answer: C.
Ligamentous injury without fracture needs rigid immobilisation, such as a halo vest, for effective stabilisation.

A 7-year-old boy falls onto his outstretched hand and sustains a greenstick fracture of the distal radius. What anatomical difference explains this injury pattern?
A. Children have thicker periosteum allowing bending fractures
B. Adults have more elastic bones
C. Children lack periosteum
D. Adults have more vascular bones
E. Children have brittle bones
Answer: A.
Thicker periosteum in children allows bending injuries like greenstick fractures that rarely occur in adults.
An 11-year-old girl with a fall has a buckle (torus) fracture of the tibia. Which property explains its formation?
A. Bones are softer and more pliable
B. Bones are brittle
C. Lack of periosteum
D. Bones are rigid
E. High bone density
Answer: A.
Paediatric bones are more flexible, leading to buckle fractures under compressive forces.
A 12-year-old boy presents after twisting his ankle; X-ray shows a fracture that crosses the physis without metaphyseal or epiphyseal involvement. What Salter–Harris type is this?
A. Type I
B. Type II
C. Type III
D. Type IV
E. Type V
Answer: A.
Type I injuries traverse the growth plate only, true to the Salter-Harris classification.
A 14-year-old girl has a distal femur fracture extending through metaphysis and physis but sparing the epiphysis. What type is it?
A. Type I
B. Type II
C. Type III
D. Type IV
E. Type V
Answer: B.
Type II fractures involve the metaphysis and physis, sparing the epiphysis.
A 13-year-old boy fractures the distal tibial physis and epiphysis through the joint surface. What Salter–Harris type describes this?
A. Type III
B. Type I
C. Type II
D. Type IV
E. Type V
Answer: A.
Type III injuries traverse the physis and enter the epiphysis, affecting the joint surface.
A 46-year-old has a distal radius fracture treated with K-wires. What is the primary advantage of K-wire fixation?
A. Provides load-bearing support
B. Minimally invasive, temporary stabilisation
C. Permanent fracture fixation
D. Replaces wrist joint
E. Allows immediate weight-bearing
Solution:
Answer: B. K-wires offer minimally invasive fixation, ideal for less complex distal radius fractures.
 
A patient with a distal radius fracture has a volar plate implanted. What is the main benefit of plate fixation over K-wires?
A. Avoids hospitalisation
B. Rigid fixation, earlier motion
C. Less invasive than K-wires
D. Cheaper
E. No need for physiotherapy
Solution:
Answer: B. Volar plates provide stable fixation, facilitating early rehabilitation and better alignment.
